h1: The IBD General Certificate in Packaging explained
title: IBD General Certificate in Packaging | Craft Beer School
desc: What the IBD General Certificate in Packaging covers, who it suits and how to prepare, with the key packaging numbers explained.
teaser: Most beer quality problems show up after the beer leaves the tank. The IBD packaging certificate is about exactly that part.
standfirst: The IBD General Certificate in Packaging is an entry level qualification for people who work on or around packaging lines. It covers how beer gets from bright tank to bottle, can and keg without losing quality. Here is what it involves and how to prepare.
sections: Packaging is where good beer gets ruined

A brewery can make an excellent beer and then damage it in the last ten minutes. Oxygen picked up during filling, poor pasteurisation control, a leaking crown or a fill height below the declared volume all reach the customer. Packaging is also where most of a brewery's labour, machinery and material cost sits.

The Institute of Brewing and Distilling (IBD) offers a General Certificate in Packaging (GCP) for people who work in this part of the brewery. It sits alongside the General Certificate in Brewing at the first level of the IBD's qualifications. Our guide to the General Certificate in Brewing covers its sister exam.

The GCP suits packaging operators, shift leaders, maintenance technicians, quality staff and brewers who want to understand the line better. It also helps people moving into packaging from engineering or another industry, because it gives them the beer-specific context.

You do not need a degree. You do need some exposure to packaging to make sense of the material. Studying it with no line experience at all is possible, but harder, because much of the syllabus describes equipment you need to picture.

The exact syllabus is set by the IBD and changes from time to time, so download the current version. In broad terms it covers:

  • Beer treatment before packaging, including filtration, stabilisation and carbonation.
  • Packaging materials: glass, cans, crowns, ends, labels, kegs and secondary packaging.
  • Bottle and can filling, including how fillers control oxygen pickup and fill levels.
  • Pasteurisation, both tunnel and flash.
  • Kegging: keg washing, filling and handling.
  • Quality control, line efficiency, hygiene and safety.

A handful of figures come up again and again in packaging work:

  • Pasteurisation units. One pasteurisation unit (PU) is one minute at 60 °C. Many lagers are tunnel pasteurised to somewhere around 15 to 25 PU, depending on the beer and the brewery's policy.
  • Dissolved oxygen. Brewers aim to keep oxygen as low as possible. Bright beer is often held below about 50 parts per billion before filling, because every bit of oxygen in the pack speeds staling.
  • Carbonation. Typically measured in grams per litre or volumes of CO2. Many lagers sit around 2.5 to 2.7 volumes, or about 5 g/L.
  • Line efficiency. The share of planned time the line actually produces saleable packs. It is the number managers watch most closely.

Knowing what these mean and what moves them is the heart of the exam.

Fill height is another figure worth understanding properly. A 330 ml bottle or can must contain at least what the label declares, within the tolerance the law allows. Underfilling short-changes the customer and can bring trouble with legal metrology officials. Overfilling gives beer away, which adds up fast on a line running thousands of packs an hour.

Indian conditions make packaging harder. Returnable glass is common in the mass market, so bottle washers and empty bottle inspection matter a great deal. Damaged or dirty returned bottles are a real risk to product quality and safety. Heat in the supply chain makes oxygen control and pasteurisation more important, because a beer that might hold up for months in a cool market can stale quickly in a hot warehouse.

Craft breweries in India increasingly can their beer on small lines. These lines are less automated, so operator skill matters more. Understanding why a can seam must be measured, or why a slow filler picks up oxygen, makes a direct difference to shelf life.

Start with the syllabus and your own line. For every topic, find where it happens in your brewery and who knows it best. Ask the maintenance engineer to show you the filler valves. Ask quality how they measure fill heights and seam dimensions. Write short notes in your own words.

  • Spread study over two to three months at a few hours a week.
  • Learn the equipment by drawing it: a simple sketch of a filler or a tunnel pasteuriser fixes it in memory.
  • Practise the basic calculations, such as PU from time and temperature, until they are automatic.
  • Use any past questions or sample papers the IBD provides.

The weak point for most candidates is the beer itself. Packaging staff often know the machines well and the product less well: why oxygen matters chemically, why some beers are more fragile than others, what haze and flavour instability really are.

The GCP is a recognised first step for packaging careers. People who pass it often move into shift leader or line supervisor roles. Some go on to the IBD Diploma in Packaging. It pairs well with engineering skills for anyone heading towards a packaging engineer career.

Your first step: ask your quality team for last month's dissolved oxygen and fill height results from your line, then find out which shift or product had the worst numbers and why.
faqs: What is the IBD General Certificate in Packaging?
It is an entry level qualification from the Institute of Brewing and Distilling covering beer treatment, packaging materials, filling, pasteurisation, kegging and quality on packaging lines.
One pasteurisation unit is the effect of holding beer at 60 °C for one minute. Breweries set a PU target for each beer to make it microbiologically stable.
Do I need to work on a packaging line to pass?
It is not required, but line experience makes the material much easier to understand because much of the syllabus describes equipment and processes.
